slides.title: What the devil are polar coordinates?

transcription.tex: A polar point \((r,\theta)\) is a distance \(r\) from the pole, at angle \(\theta\) anticlockwise from the initial line. Angles are in radians.\par Convert the Cartesian point \((4,3)\) to polar form.
\[r=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5,\quad \theta=\arctan(3/4)\approx0.644\]The point is \((5,0.644)\). Add multiples of \(2\pi\) to obtain equivalent angles.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

slides.title: Why polar form sometimes are preferable

transcription.tex: \textbf{A spiral: }\(r=\theta\), \(\theta\ge0\).\par As the angle increases, the distance from the pole increases.\par Its parametric form is \(x=\theta\cos\theta,\ y=\theta\sin\theta\).
An inverse-trigonometric expression loses angle information: \(\arccos(x/r)\) returns only angles from 0 to \(\pi\). It does not describe the complete multi-turn spiral.

transcription.tex: 5. Prove the distance formula for polar points \(P=(r_1,\theta_1)\), \(Q=(r_2,\theta_2)\).

\[PQ^2=(r_2\cos\theta_2-r_1\cos\theta_1)^2\]\[\phantom{PQ^2={}}+(r_2\sin\theta_2-r_1\sin\theta_1)^2\]\[=r_1^2+r_2^2-2r_1r_2\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)\]Take the non-negative square root. Alternatively, apply the cosine rule to triangle OPQ.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Recognising polar curves}\par \(r=a\): circle, centre the pole, radius \(a\).\par \(\theta=\alpha\), \(r\ge0\): a ray from the pole.\par \(r=a\theta\), \(\theta\ge0\): an Archimedean spiral.\par Plot points and mark the direction of increasing angle.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exploration}\par Plot \(r=\cos(3\theta/4)\), allowing signed radii, for \(0\le\theta\le8\pi\).\par A negative radius is plotted in the opposite direction. This extension is separate from our usual \(r\ge0\) convention.
The trigonometric expression and the direction both repeat after \(8\pi\). Rational frequency ratios produce closed patterns.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Limaçons}\par \(r=a(p+q\cos\theta)\), with \(a,q>0\), \(p\ge q\).\par \(p=q\): cardioid with a cusp.\par \(q<p<2q\): dimpled limaçon.\par \(p\ge2q\): convex limaçon.\par The curve is symmetric in the initial line.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: a. Convex: radii at \(0,\pi/2,\pi\) are \(7a,5a,3a\).\par b. Dimpled: corresponding radii are \(5a,3a,a\).

\[(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=25\]\[r^2-6r\cos\theta-8r\sin\theta=0\]\[r=6\cos\theta+8\sin\theta\]The circle passes through the pole; include it when the radius is zero.

transcription.tex: 3a. Sketch \(|z-12-5i|=13\) on an Argand diagram.\par b. Show its polar equation is \(r=24\cos\theta+10\sin\theta\).
A circle centred at \((12,5)\), radius 13; it passes through the origin.
\[(r\cos\theta-12)^2+(r\sin\theta-5)^2=169\]\[r^2=24r\cos\theta+10r\sin\theta\]Divide by \(r\) away from the pole; the polar curve also includes the pole.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Curve summary}\par \(r=a\): circle at the pole.\par \(\theta=\alpha\): ray at angle \(\alpha\).\par \(r=2a\cos\theta\): circle centred at \((a,0)\), radius \(a\).\par \(r=k\theta\): spiral.\par Always state the angular interval and whether signed radii are permitted.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Symmetry and orientation}\par \(a(1+\cos\theta)\): cardioid facing right.\par \(a(1-\cos\theta)\): cardioid facing left.\par Replacing cosine by sine rotates the orientation.\par \(a(3+2\cos\theta)\): a dimpled limaçon, with minimum radius \(a\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{More standard forms}\par \(r=a\cos2\theta\), \(r\ge0\): two positive-radius petals.\par \(r^2=a^2\cos2\theta\): lemniscate.\par \(r=p\sec(\alpha-\theta)\): straight line\par \(x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=p\).\par In particular, \(r=a\sec\theta\) gives \(x=a\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{From strips to sectors}\par In Cartesian coordinates, area is accumulated from thin strips: \(dA=y\,dx\).\par A solid of revolution uses thin discs: \(dV=\pi y^2dx\).\par For polar area, use thin sectors with angle \(d\theta\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Area in polar coordinates}\par A sector of radius \(r\) and angle \(d\theta\) has area approximately \(\frac12r^2d\theta\).
\[A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta\]Choose limits that trace the required region once. Split the integral where the boundary changes; use symmetry when appropriate.

Use only the outer turn so the inner region is not counted twice.\[A=\frac12\int_{2\pi}^{4\pi}\left(\frac{3\theta}{7\pi}\right)^2d\theta=\frac{12\pi}7\ \mathrm{cm}^2\]

transcription.tex: Explain why \(r=a(p+q\cos\theta)\), \(p>q>0\), has a dimple when \(p<2q\).

\[x=a(p\cos\theta+q\cos^2\theta)\]\[\frac{dx}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta(p+2q\cos\theta)\]Besides \(\theta=0,\pi\), an extra pair of vertical tangents occurs when \(\cos\theta=-p/(2q)\). This is possible precisely when \(q<p<2q\), producing the dimple.
